title: Surface Forces: Weathering and Erosion
summary: Internal and external forces that shape the land, physical, chemical and biological weathering, and erosion by water, wind, ice and the sea.

notes.text: The Earth's surface is shaped by two groups of forces. **Internal forces** (from inside the Earth), such as folding, faulting, earthquakes and volcanoes, **build up** the land. **External (surface) forces**, mainly weathering and erosion, **wear down** the land.

rows: Weathering
The breaking down of rock in place (it does not move)
Erosion
The wearing away and removal of rock and soil by an agent such as water, wind or ice
Transport
The carrying of eroded material
Deposition
The dropping of material when the agent loses energy

notes.text: Rock is broken into smaller pieces without any change in its chemical make-up.

items: **Frost action (freeze–thaw)**: water enters cracks, freezes and expands by about 9%, widening the crack. Repeated freezing and thawing breaks the rock. Common in the Drakensberg in winter.

**Exfoliation (onion-skin weathering)**: in hot deserts, rock surfaces heat up by day and cool at night. The outer layers expand and contract more than the inside and peel off in sheets, leaving rounded rocks.
**Pressure release**: when overlying rock is eroded, the rock beneath expands and cracks in layers.
**Salt crystal growth**: salt water evaporates in cracks, and the growing crystals push the rock apart (common on coasts).

notes.caption: Frost action: water in a crack freezes and expands, and repeated freezing breaks the rock.

notes.title: How frost splits a rock
notes.problem: Explain why rocks in the Drakensberg crack in winter.
steps: Rain seeps into cracks in the rock.
At night the water freezes and expands by about 9%, forcing the crack wider.
It melts and the cycle repeats until pieces break off.
notes.answer: This is frost action, a type of physical weathering.

notes.text: Minerals in the rock react with water, oxygen or acids and change into new substances, weakening the rock. It is fastest in **hot, wet** climates.

items: **Carbonation**: rainwater containing carbon dioxide forms a weak acid that dissolves limestone, forming caves such as the Sudwala Caves and the Cango Caves.
**Oxidation**: iron minerals react with oxygen and water to form rust-coloured iron oxide, making rocks red-brown and crumbly.
**Hydrolysis**: water reacts with minerals such as feldspar in granite, changing them into clay.

notes.title: How limestone caves form
notes.problem: Explain how rainwater can hollow out limestone, as at the Sudwala and Cango caves.
steps: Rain absorbs carbon dioxide and becomes a weak carbonic acid.
The acid reacts with limestone and dissolves it.
Over many thousands of years the gaps grow into caves.

items: Plant **roots** grow into cracks and force them open.
Burrowing animals and **earthworms** expose rock to more weathering.
**Lichens** and decaying plants produce acids that break down rock.

rows: Running water (rivers)
Fast-flowing rivers carry rocks that grind the bed and banks; most important agent in South Africa
V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, gorges; deposition forms flood plains and deltas
Wind
Blows away loose sand and dust; sand blasting shapes rocks; strongest in dry areas
Sand dunes, mushroom (pedestal) rocks
Ice (glaciers)
Moving ice plucks and grinds rock
U-shaped valleys (not in South Africa today)
The sea (waves)
Waves pound and wear away the coast
Cliffs, caves, arches, stacks; deposition forms beaches and spits

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Climate determines the main type of weathering: **physical** weathering dominates in **dry and cold** areas (deserts, mountains), and **chemical** weathering dominates in **hot and wet** areas (tropics, KZN coast).
